title: Prediction of Adverse Events in Single Ventricle Physiology Infants Using Artificial Intelligence Tools. - Model 1 (Decision Tree)
full_text_url: Prediction of Adverse Events in Single Ventricle Physiology Infants Using Artificial Intelligence Tools
study_aim: To develop and evaluate machine learning models using continuous physiologic data to predict and identify adverse events (cardiac arrest, ECMO cannulation, and endotracheal intubation) up to 8 hours before occurrence in single ventricle infants, under the CARDIO-SV framework
setting: Cardiac ICU (CICU), Children's National Hospital, tertiary care center
age_groups: Neonates and Infants (<6 months old at CICU admission) no further split, who had not yet received a bidirectional GLenn proceudre at the time of admission to CICU
sample_size: 158 patients (324 admissions); observation-window subsets: 8hr n=119, 4hr n=112, 2hr n=108, 1hr n=103
conditions: Single ventricle physiology — hypoplastic left heart syndrome (39.87%), tricuspid atresia (13.29%), heterotaxy syndrome (8.86%), mitral atresia (7.59%), unbalanced atrioventricular canal (7.59%), pulmonary atresia/intact ventricular septum (7.59%), other SV (6.32%), double inlet left ventricle (5.69%), Shone's syndrome (2.53%), total anomalous pulmonary venous connection (0.63%)
modality_raw: Vital signs (heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, temperature, central venous pressure)
feature_selection: 15 variables initially extracted, narrowed to 6 "high-quality" variables continuously available across patients; no formal automated selection algorithm described
time_series: Yes — continuous physiologic monitoring (5-second sampling), segmented into 1/2/4/8-hour windows, each treated as an independent instance
internal_validation: Ten-fold cross-validation on training set for hyperparameter tuning (grid search); 90% training/validation (80% training, 10% validation within that) / 10% held-out test split
split_sizes: 90% training/validation (80%/10% split within), 10% held-out test; exact counts not reported
frequency_raw: Not explicitly continuous; each window treated as an independent snapshot instance
lead_time_raw: Up to 8 hours before AE; windows tested at 1, 2, 4, 8 hours
outcome_raw: Adverse event defined as unplanned intubation, ECMO cannulation, ECPR, or cardiac arrest in the CICU; binary AE vs non-AE for Detect framework

title: Early identification of impending cardiac arrest in neonates and infants in the cardiovascular ICU: a statistical mo
full_text_url: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/cardiology-in-the-young/article/abs/early-identification-of-impending-cardiac-arrest-in-neonates-and-infants-in-the-cardiovascular-icu-a-statistical-modelling-approach-using-physiologic-monitoring-data/85284A8329228A956251C8D1EC252CE1
study_aim: To develop a physiological data-driven statistical model for early identification of impending cardiac arrest in neonates and infants with cardiac disease hospitalised in the cardiovascular ICU
setting: Cardiovascular ICU, Johns Hopkins All Children's Hospital (JHACH), St. Petersburg, FL, a tertiary care children's hospital
recruitment: Reported inconsistently within the document: abstract states 11/01/2013–16/09/2015, while Methods states 01/11/2013 and 16/09/2015; flagged as a discrepancy in the source document
age: Not reported (only age range specified as ≤1 year old; no mean/median value given)
age_groups: Neonates and Infants (≤1 year old, per inclusion criteria)
sample_size: 22 cardiac arrest and 206 control patients ≤1 year old in the original cohort; after excluding 6 cardiac arrest patients with insufficient pre-arrest data, the model was trained and evaluated on 16 cardiac arrest cases and 48 age/gender-matched controls (1:3 ratio) — 11 cardiac arrest + 33 controls in training, 5 cardiac arrest + 15 controls in test
ca_prevalence: 9.6% (pre-test probability; 22 cardiac arrest patients among 228 total in the original cohort)
conditions: Cardiac disease/congenital heart disease (CHD), not further broken down by specific diagnosis
architecture_raw: Logistic regression (baseline comparator) — described in the paper as a "generalized linear model" for a Bernoulli distribution, mathematically equivalent to logistic regression, though the paper does not use that exact term
modality_raw: Multimodal (vital signs: heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure; plus ECG waveform-derived heart rate variability measures and premature ventricular contraction rate)
feature_selection: Feature selection method: Not a formal automated selection algorithm; features retained based on model weight magnitude and statistical significance (p<0.05) from the fitted model (see Fig 2)
predictors: Number of predictors: 16 features (age, gender, heart rate, HR-corr, respiratory rate, RR-corr, heart rate variability, SpO2, premature ventricular contraction rate, HRV-VLF, HRV-LF, HRV-HF, HRV ratio HF/LF, rVLF, rLF, rHF — full list and definitions in Table 1)
time_series: Yes — minute-to-minute physiologic monitoring data; training window lengths of 1–7 hours tested, optimal training window of 2 hours selected
internal_validation: Train/test split (11 CA+33 controls training; 5 CA+15 controls test) with bootstrapping (60 iterations) to estimate standard error/confidence intervals; ROC-curve-derived optimal threshold selected on training set and applied to test set;
external_validation_raw: Not reported (none performed; authors state future multi-institutional prospective validation is needed)
split_sizes: Training: 11 cardiac arrest + 33 controls (44 total); Test: 5 cardiac arrest + 15 controls (20 total)
frequency_raw: Continuous (minute-by-minute risk score)
sensitivity_raw: 60.6% (test set; unchanged when evaluated on entire dataset excluding patients with <2h data)

title: Early Changes in Near-Infrared Spectroscopy Are Associated With Cardiac Arrest in Children With Congenital Heart Disease
full_text_url: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/pediatrics/articles/10.3389/fped.2022.894125/full
study_aim: To determine if a model utilizing regional cerebral oximetry (rSO2c) and somatic oximetry (rSO2s), alongside other clinical variables, could predict cardiac arrest (CA) in children admitted to a single-center pediatric cardiac intensive care unit (CICU).
setting: Pediatric cardiac intensive care unit (CICU), Children's Medical Center Dallas — a 26-bed unit admitting surgical and non-surgical patients with heart disease
age:
Cardiac arrest group: median 54 days [IQR 1–908 days
 No cardiac arrest (control) group: median 217 days [IQR 30–1,563]; P < 0.0001
age_groups: Mixed — reported as median age in days with wide IQR spanning neonates through older children
sex:
Cardiac arrest group: 76/160 (47.5%) female (calculated from 84/160 = 52.50% male)
Control group: 344/711 (48.38%) female (calculated from 367/711 = 51.62% male); P = 0.84 (not significant)
sample_size: 160 cardiac arrest (case) patients; 711 control patients; total N = 871
ca_prevalence: 160/871 (18.4%) in this case-control cohort (not a natural population prevalence, as cases and controls were selected via case-control design)
conditions: Congenital heart disease (surgical and non-surgical patients); single ventricle physiology significantly more common in CA group (64/160, 40.0%) vs. controls (91/711, 12.80%), P < 0.0001; for surgical patients, CA group had higher STAT mortality categories, longer CPB times (median 118.0 vs. 77.0 minutes, P < 0.0001), and longer cross-clamp times (median 70.0 vs. 49.5 minutes, P = 0.003)
architecture_raw: Logistic regression (baseline comparator) — described as a multivariable logistic regression model
modality_raw: Multimodal — vital signs, laboratory values, and NIRS (near-infrared spectroscopy) oximetry data (rSO2c, rSO2s), plus vasoactive medication data (VIS)
feature_selection: The 11 candidate variables were originally selected via a previously created XGBoost machine-learning algorithm (from a separate, unpublished study by the same group); of these, univariable analysis was performed on each variable, and only those significantly associated with CA were carried forward into the multivariable logistic regression model
predictors: 11 candidate variables considered (HR, SpO2, DBP, rSO2c, rSO2s, ETCO2, urine output, base excess, anion gap, FiO2, VIS); final multivariable model included 5 variables (SpO2-rSO2c difference, SpO2-rSO2s difference, HR, DBP, VIS); of these, 4 were independently significantly associated with CA (SpO2-rSO2s difference, HR, VIS, DBP) — SpO2-rSO2c difference was not significant
time_series: Yes — hourly averaged data analyzed across hours 1 through 15 prior to CA (for cases) or within the first 48 hours of admission (for controls); model performance (AUROC) calculated as a function of time before arrest
internal_validation: NR
split_sizes: NR
frequency_raw: Hourly snapshot — hourly averaged values used, model evaluated at discrete hourly time points from 15 hours to 1 hour before CA (not continuous/high-frequency)
auroc_raw: 0.83 at 1 hour before CA (best/peak performance); AUROC increased over time as it approached the arrest, ranging from approximately 0.72–0.74 at 15–10 hours prior, rising to 0.83 at 1 hour prior (see Figure 1 for full hourly trend)
lead_time_raw: Evaluated at each hour from 1 to 15 hours prior to CA; peak/best performance reported at 1 hour prior to CA
outcome_raw: Actual arrest — cardiac arrest defined per the Get With The Guidelines Resuscitation (GWTGR) Registry as pulselessness or pulse with inadequate perfusion requiring chest compressions and/or defibrillation; study included only arrests resulting in chest compressions (excluded defibrillation-only events without compressions); index events only, confirmed via EHR chart review
